etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English tagge (“small piece hanging from a garment”), probably of North Germanic origin. Compare Norwegian tagg (“point; prong; barb; tag”), Swedish tagg (“thorn; prickle; tine”), Icelandic tág (“a willow-twig”). Compare also tack.

definitions.definition: A small label.
A skin tag, an excrescence of skin.
A dangling lock of sheep's wool, matted with dung; a dung tag.
Any slight appendage, as to an article of dress; something slight hanging loosely.
A metallic binding, tube, or point, at the end of a string, or lace, to stiffen it.
(biochemistry) Any short peptide sequence artificially attached to proteins mostly in order to help purify, solubilize or visualize these proteins.
Something mean and paltry; the rabble, originally refer to rag as torn cloth.

quote.citation: 1596 (date written; published 1633), Edmund Spenser, A Vewe of the Present State of Irelande […], Dublin:  […]  Societie of Stationers, […], →OCLC; republished as A View of the State of Ireland […] (Ancient Irish Histories), Dublin:  […]  Society of Stationers,  […]  Hibernia Press,  […]  [b]y John Morrison, 1809, →OCLC:
quote.text: For upon the like Proclamation there, they all came in, both tag and rag

definitions.definition: (heading) Physical appendage.
(music) The last line (or last two lines) of a song's chorus that is repeated to indicate the end of the song.
(television) The last scene of a TV program, often focusing on the program's subplot.

quote.citation: 2006, Stephen V. Duncan, A Guide to Screenwriting Success, page 300:
quote.text: Often, the tag punctuates the "we're all in this together" theme and is topped with a laugh.

definitions.definition: The end, or catchword, of an actor's speech; cue.
(heading) Last nonphysical appendage.
(informal, authorship) An attribution in narrated dialogue (eg, "he said") or attributed words (e.g. "he thought").

quote.citation: (Can we date this quote?), michael, alt.fiction.original‎[1] (Usenet):
quote.text: Seems here like Russ would be speaking. You could use a tag here.

quote.citation: (Can we date this quote?), Jane MacDonald, alt.fiction.original‎[2] (Usenet):
quote.text: If you want to start with talk, stick a tag in right away

quote.citation: (Can we date this quote?), bart_...@hotmail.com, alt.fiction.original‎[3] (Usenet):
quote.text: You could combine these two paragraphs, I think, and rewrite to lose the tag portion of the third sentence.

definitions.definition: (computing) A piece of markup representing an element in a markup language.
(computing) A keyword, term, or phrase associated with or assigned to data, media, and/or information enabling keyword-based classification; often used to categorize content.
(heading) Nonphysical label.
(chiefly US) A vehicle number plate; a medal bearing identification data (animals, soldiers).
(slang) A person's name.
(heading) Identity.

(uncountable) A game, especially for children on playgrounds, in which one player (known as "it") attempts to touch another, who then becomes "it"; any similar game of chasing and trying to reach, touch, shoot, or label other players.
(baseball) An instance of touching the baserunner with the ball or the ball in a gloved hand to rule him "out."
(heading) Involving being tagged physically.
Graffiti in the form of a stylized signature particular to the artist.

quote.citation: 2011, Scape Martinez, Graff 2: Next Level Graffiti Techniques, page 124:
quote.text: There is a hierarchy of sorts: a throw-up can go over a tag, a piece over a throw-up, and a burner over a piece.

definitions.definition: (heading) Signature.
A type of cardboard.
A sheep in its first year.

quote.citation: 1807, The Complete Farmer, or, General Dictionary of Agriculture and Husbandry, →OCLC:
quote.text: After being weaned, the ram or wedder lamb is sometimes termed hog, hoggit, or tag, during the whole of the first year

definitions.definition: (transitive) To label (something).
(transitive) To mark (something) with one's graffiti tag.
(transitive) To remove dung tags from a sheep.
(transitive, baseball, colloquial) To hit the ball hard.
(transitive, vulgar, slang, 1990s) to have sex with someone (especially a man of a woman)
(transitive, baseball) To put a runner out by touching them with the ball or the ball in a gloved hand.
(transitive, computing) To mark with a tag (metadata for classification).
(transitive, Internet) To attach the name of (a user) to a posted message so that they are linked from the post and possibly sent a notification.

quote.citation: 2021, Julie B. Wiest, Theorizing Criminality and Policing in the Digital Media Age, page 82:
quote.text: One side wants to demonstrate a higher level of street knowledge and openly denounces the distorting lens of Instagram dissings; the other embraces the medium's branding affordances by sending “clout” to a third-party ally, while at the same time avoiding tagging the opponent.

definitions.definition: To follow closely, accompany, tag along.

quote.citation: 1906 April, O. Henry [pseudonym; William Sydney Porter], “By Courier”, in The Four Million, New York, N.Y.: McClure, Phillips & Co, →OCLC:
quote.text: A tall young man came striding through the park along the path near which she sat. Behind him tagged a boy carrying a suit-case.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To catch and touch (a player in the game of tag).
(transitive) To fit with, or as if with, a tag or tags.

quote.citation: 1911, Thomas Babington Macaulay, “Bunyan, John”, in 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica‎[4]:
quote.text: He learned to make long-tagged thread laces.

quote.citation: 1693, Decimus Junius Juvenalis, John Dryden, transl., “[The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis.] The Eighth Satyr”, in The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis. Translated into English Verse.  […]  Together with the Satires of Aulus Persius Flaccus. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], →OCLC:
quote.text: His courteous host  […]  / Tags every sentence with some fawning word.

definitions.definition: To fasten; to attach.

quote.citation: a. 1751, Henry St John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke, an essay
quote.text: they began to tag their law with the scraps of philofophy

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Aramaic תגא (taga, “crown”). Doublet of taj.

definitions.definition: A decoration drawn over some Hebrew letters in Jewish scrolls.
